intro.h1: Plan your Wi-Fi mesh on your floor plan
intro.p: Planejador WiFi shows where the signal reaches before you buy a router: draw the walls, place the router and mesh nodes, and see the coverage on 2.4, 5 and 6 GHz. Free, no sign-up, and your projects stay in your browser.

guide.howToSteps:
• Click Start my project (or New project) and give it a name. The sheet opens at 16 × 12 m; change its size under File › Plan and scale if needed.
  • If you have the floor plan as a photo or an image, load it under File › Plan and scale and set the scale with Measure.
  • With the Wall tool, click each corner: walls follow one another, and clicking the first point closes the room. Rectangle draws a whole room at once. Pick the material; doors and windows are walls too, made of wood or glass.
  • With Router, place the main router where the ISP modem is, then the other nodes.
  • Switch between 2.4, 5 and 6 GHz and look at the heat map. Green is excellent signal; red is no usable signal.
  • Use Suggest a spot to find where one more node helps most, and File › Export JSON to keep the project.
guide.wallsTitle: How much each wall takes from the signal
guide.wallsText: Every wall the signal crosses adds a loss in decibels (dB). Each 10 dB cuts the received power to one tenth, so two or three brick walls already make a difference. The values below are the averages the planner uses; real loss depends on thickness, moisture and steel reinforcement.
guide.signalText: Wi-Fi signal is measured in dBm and is always negative: the closer to zero, the better.
guide.bandsText:
2.4 GHz reaches farther and goes through walls better, but it is slow and shared with your neighbors. Good for smart-home devices and far corners.

5 GHz is the everyday balance: much faster, with medium range. Check the map on this band first.

6 GHz, found on Wi-Fi 6E and tri-band Wi-Fi 7 routers, is the fastest and least crowded, but loses more at every wall. It shines in the router's own room and on the link between mesh nodes.
signalUse: 4K streaming, online gaming and the full speed of your plan.
Stable HD video and video calls. The target for rooms you use.
Browsing and messaging work; video may stutter.

faq.q: How accurate is the planner?
faq.a: It is an estimate with a typical error of 8 dB either way. Use it to compare placements and decide how many nodes to buy. After installing, confirm with a Wi-Fi analyzer app on your phone.

faq.q: How many mesh nodes do I need?
faq.a: As a rule of thumb, one node per 80 to 120 m² (860 to 1,300 sq ft) in a brick house, and one per floor in multi-story homes. Concrete walls, slabs and long houses need more. Draw your plan and use Suggest a spot to see whether another node pays off.

faq.q: Where should I put the main router?
faq.a: As close to the center of the house as possible, about 1 meter (3 ft) off the floor, away from fridges, mirrors and metal cabinets. If the modem sits in a corner, run a network cable to a central spot or put a mesh node there.

faq.q: Is a Wi-Fi 7 mesh with 6 GHz worth it?
faq.a: The 6 GHz band is fast and uncrowded but goes through walls poorly. It is most useful for the link between nodes and for devices in the same room. For internet plans up to 1 Gbps, a dual-band Wi-Fi 7 mesh is usually enough.

faq.q: Wired or wireless backhaul?
faq.a: Wired whenever you can: speed does not drop and nodes can sit farther apart. Wirelessly, aim for −60 to −70 dBm between nodes. Below that, devices connected to the far node get much slower.

faq.q: Where are my projects saved?
faq.a: Only in your browser, in the device's local storage. Nothing is sent to a server. To keep a copy or open it on another computer, use File and then Export JSON.

privacy.noCookies: This site uses no cookies and no third-party tracking tools.
privacy.rightsText: You can ask for information about how your data is processed, or for its deletion, at contato@planejadorwifi.com.
privacy.linksText: The Copy link button puts the whole project inside the link itself, in the part after the # sign. That part is never sent to the server: whoever opens the link gets the regular page, and the browser reads the project right there, saves it as a new project and removes that part from the address bar. The floor-plan image is not included in the link. Anyone with the link can see the project, so share it only with people you choose.

router.title: Where to Put Your Wi-Fi Router at Home | Planejador WiFi
router.description: The best spot for a router is the middle of the home, 1 to 2 m off the floor and away from metal. See how much each wall cuts its range and what to do if the modem is in a corner.
router.h1: Where should you put your Wi-Fi router?
router.answer:
Put the router in the middle of your home, 1 to 2 meters off the floor, out in the open and away from metal, mirrors and the fridge. The best spot is the one with the fewest walls between the router and the rooms where you use the internet most.

Walls matter more than distance. In the Planejador WiFi model, good 5 GHz signal reaches about {range.b5} m with nothing in the way, {range.b5.tijolo} m through one brick wall and {range.b5.tijolo.2} m through two.

If your ISP’s modem sits in a corner, bring the router to the middle with a network cable or use a mesh system. In a two-story home the floor slab takes {db.slab.b5} dB off the 5 GHz signal, and one node per floor usually solves it.

sections.q: Why is the middle of the home the best spot?
sections.html:
A router sends its signal out in every direction, roughly evenly. From a corner, half of it goes to the street or the neighbors, and the room on the far side gets both the longest distance and the most walls.

From the middle, the distance to the farthest room is cut in half, and most rooms end up one or two walls away. “Middle” means the middle of where you use the internet: if the office and the living room are on one side and the garage on the other, move the router toward the side that matters.

sections.q: What matters more: distance or walls?
sections.html:
Walls. Each wall takes off a fixed number of decibels, and the signal lost that way is worth many meters of distance. In the planner’s model, one brick wall divides the distance at which 5 GHz signal stays good by {factor.b5.tijolo}; a concrete wall divides it by {factor.b5.concreto}.

  • No walls: good signal up to about {range.b5} m on 5 GHz and {range.b24} m on 2.4 GHz.
  • One brick wall: {range.b5.tijolo} m on 5 GHz and {range.b24.tijolo} m on 2.4 GHz.
  • Two brick walls: {range.b5.tijolo.2} m on 5 GHz and {range.b24.tijolo.2} m on 2.4 GHz.
  • One concrete wall or pillar: {range.b5.concreto} m on 5 GHz.

So when you pick a spot, count the walls between the router and each room before you measure the distance. “Good signal” here means {level.1} dBm or better, enough for HD video and video calls.

sections.q: How high should the router be?
sections.html: Between 1 and 2 meters off the floor, on a shelf or mounted on the wall, with open space around it. On the floor, the signal has to get through furniture and people before it reaches your devices. On a high shelf, it clears most of the furniture.

sections.q: What should you keep away from the router?
sections.html:
• Metal, mirrors and the fridge: they reflect and block the signal. The model counts {db.metal.b5} dB on 5 GHz for them; a concrete wall counts {db.concreto.b5} dB.
  • Aquariums and water tanks: water absorbs Wi-Fi frequencies well.
  • Microwave ovens: they run near 2.4 GHz and disturb that band while they are on.
  • Behind the TV or inside an AV cabinet: TVs have metal backs, and the cabinet surrounds the router with electronics.

sections.q: What if the ISP’s modem is in a corner?
sections.html:
The modem goes where the ISP’s cable or fiber comes in, and that is rarely the middle of the home. There are three ways out, from simplest to most complete:

  1. A network cable to the middle: run a network cable (Cat 5e or Cat 6) from the modem to a router in the middle of the home, and turn off the modem’s Wi-Fi so two networks don’t compete for the same space.
  2. A mesh system: the main node sits next to the modem, connected by cable, and a second node goes near the middle or the far side. The nodes talk to each other wirelessly or, better, over a cable.
  3. Move the ISP’s outlet: ask the technician to install the modem somewhere more central on the next visit.

sections.q: Where should it go in a two-story home?
sections.html:
The slab between floors takes {db.slab.b5} dB off the 5 GHz signal and {db.slab.b24} dB off 2.4 GHz, more than most walls. With the router downstairs, good 5 GHz signal reaches about {range.b5.slab} m in a straight line upstairs, before counting any walls up there.

If one floor gets much more use, put the router there. If both do, a high spot in the middle of the ground floor (near the ceiling, on a tall bookcase) helps, but the most reliable setup is one mesh node per floor, ideally one above the other and, if you can, wired together.

sections.q: How do you know the spot works?
sections.html:
Measure the signal strength, in dBm, in the rooms you use most. Aim for {level.1} dBm or better; {level.0} dBm or better is excellent. Below {level.2} dBm the connection gets slow and unstable.

The Wi-Fi signal strength in dBm guide shows how to measure it on Android, iPhone, Mac and Windows.

Before you drill a hole or buy cable, try the spots in the planner: draw your floor plan, move the router around and compare the signal map for each option.

faq.q: Can I hide the router in a cabinet?
faq.a: You can, but it loses range. A wooden door takes {db.madeira.b5} dB off 5 GHz and a metal cabinet or rack {db.metal.b5} dB, which can cost a whole room of coverage. If you need to hide it, use open shelving or leave the door open.

faq.q: Should the router’s antennas point up?
faq.a: On most routers, yes. External antennas spread the signal more to the sides than up and down, so upright antennas cover the same floor best. In a two-story home, tilting one antenna often helps the floor above. Models with internal antennas should stand the way they come in the box.

faq.q: Is one router enough, or do I need mesh?
faq.a: One router is usually enough when every room you use is at most two brick walls away from it: up to about {range.b5.tijolo.2} m with two walls in the way, on 5 GHz. Larger, long or two-story homes usually need more than one access point. The planner shows this on your own floor plan.

cta.title: Try the spot on your floor plan
cta.text: Draw your home’s walls, place the router and see the estimated signal in every room. Drag the router somewhere else and compare in seconds.

nodes.title: How Many Mesh Wi-Fi Nodes Do I Need? By Square Meter | Planejador WiFi
nodes.description: How many mesh nodes to buy for a single-story house, two-story house, apartment or long house, with coverage for homes of {area.h60} to {area.h250} m² worked out by the same model as the planner.
nodes.h1: How many mesh Wi-Fi nodes do I need?
nodes.answer:
In a single-story brick house, one well-placed mesh node is usually enough up to about {area.h120} m². In the Planejador WiFi model it gives {cover.h120.1} of that house good 5 GHz signal; at {area.h150} m² it covers {cover.h150.1}, and at {area.h200} m², {cover.h200.1}. From there on you need a second and a third node.

Floor area is only the starting point. A two-story house needs one node per floor, an apartment with concrete walls may need two even when it is small, and a long, narrow house needs more nodes than a square one of the same size.

Start with the number your floor plan calls for. If a corner turns out weak later, adding a node is easy: the mesh system picks it up on its own.

sections.q: How many nodes per square meter?
sections.html:
The table shows how much of the house gets good signal ({level.1} dBm or better) on 5 GHz with one, two and three nodes. The houses are single-story rectangles with brick walls, rooms of about {room} × {room} m and a wooden door in every inner wall. Each node was placed by the same search as the Suggest a spot button.

{table.nodes}

The last column is the number of nodes needed to get more than {target} of the area to good signal. What is left out is usually a corner against an outer wall, where hardly anyone uses a phone.

sections.q: Why does a long house need more nodes?
sections.html:
Because what counts is the distance and the number of walls to the farthest room, not the area. A {size.long} house has {area.long} m², almost the same as the {area.h150} m² house in the table, but one node covers only {cover.long.1} of it, against {cover.h150.1} in the squarer house. Two nodes bring it to {cover.long.2}, and it takes {need.long} to pass {target}.

In a long house, spread the nodes along its length, in a line, so each one reaches the next through one or two walls.

sections.q: How many nodes for a two-story house?
sections.html:
One per floor. In the example two-story house, {size.twoStory} per floor ({area.twoStory} m² in all), one node downstairs covers {cover.twoStory.1.0} of the ground floor and only {cover.twoStory.1.1} of the upper floor, because the slab takes {db.slab.b5} dB off the 5 GHz signal. With a second node upstairs, the whole house reaches {cover.twoStory.2}.

Put the nodes one above the other or near the stairs: that is the shortest path between floors. If the link between them drops below {link.1} dBm, connect the upstairs node with a cable.

sections.q: What about an apartment?
sections.html:
Apartments are smaller, but many have concrete or load-bearing masonry walls, which take {db.concreto.b5} dB off the 5 GHz signal, against {db.tijolo.b5} dB for ordinary brick. In the example apartment, {area.apartment} m² with concrete inner walls, one node covers {cover.apartment.1}; two cover {cover.apartment.2}.

In a building the neighbors matter too: dozens of networks compete for the same channels. The model does not count that interference, so treat the result as the best case and keep the main node in the middle of the apartment, not in the living room by the window.

sections.q: Are more nodes always better?
sections.html:
No. An extra node only helps if it covers an area that was weak and has a link of {link.1} dBm or better to another node. Two nodes too close together repeat the same coverage and share the same channel, and every extra wireless node is one more hop for the traffic of the nodes behind it.

In the table, look for where coverage stops rising: past that point, another node costs money and does not change the map.

sections.q: How do I work it out for my home?
sections.html:
1. Draw the walls of your home in the planner, with the material of each one.
  2. Place the main router where your ISP’s modem is.
  3. Click Suggest a spot and accept the suggestion. Repeat while the area with good signal keeps clearly rising.
  4. Check the list of links between nodes: a weak link calls for a cable or a closer node.

The number of nodes at the end is the size of the kit. If you can run a cable to one of them, mark it Connected by network cable and see whether you can do with one fewer.

faq.q: Should I buy a two-pack or a three-pack?
faq.a: Go by the result on your floor plan. If two nodes already give the house good signal, a third one will not make the network faster: it is only worth it if it covers an area left weak, such as the garage or the backyard.

faq.q: Can I mix nodes from different brands?
faq.a: Usually not: the nodes of a mesh system only network with the same brand and product line. Some models follow the Wi-Fi EasyMesh standard, which allows mixing, but support is still rare. Check the manual before you buy.

faq.q: Does my ISP’s router count as a node?
faq.a: Usually not. The common setup is to connect the main mesh node to the ISP’s router with a cable and turn off the ISP router’s Wi-Fi, so two networks do not compete for the same channels.

mesh.title: Mesh vs Extender vs Ethernet: Which Is Best for Wi-Fi? | Planejador WiFi
mesh.description: When to use a network cable, a mesh system or a Wi-Fi extender, what backhaul is and which link between devices keeps your speed, with numbers from the planner’s model.
mesh.h1: Mesh, extender or Ethernet cable: which is best?
mesh.answer:
If you can run a network cable, use it: a second router or mesh node connected by cable delivers the full speed and can go anywhere in the house. Without a cable, a mesh system is the simplest and most stable choice for a home with more than one weak room.

A plain Wi-Fi extender is the cheapest and the most limited. Many create a network with a different name, and single-radio models repeat on the same channel they receive on, which cuts the speed in half. It fixes one room, not the house.

With any wireless option, the link between the devices, the backhaul, is what matters: aim for {link.1} dBm or better. Below that, everything connected to the far device slows down.

sections.q: What is the difference between mesh and an extender?
sections.html:
A mesh system is a set of devices from one brand that act as a single network: one name, one password, one app for everything. The nodes agree among themselves on how traffic flows and nudge your phone to the nearest node as you walk around the house.

An extender is a standalone device that picks up the router’s signal and sends it out again. It does not talk to the router about who serves each device, so your phone tends to stay stuck on the weaker point until the connection drops. It works, but it takes more patience.

sections.q: What is backhaul and why does it matter?
sections.html:
Backhaul is the link between a node and the main router (or another node). All the traffic of the devices connected to a node goes through it, so a node is never faster than its backhaul.

  • {link.0} dBm or better: a great link.
  • Between {link.0} and {link.1} dBm: good enough for most homes.
  • Below {link.1} dBm: weak; connect that node with a cable or move it closer.

In the model, a 5 GHz link stays at {link.1} dBm or better up to about {linkrange.b5.tijolo} m through one brick wall and {linkrange.b5.tijolo.2} m through two. That is why a satellite node does better halfway between the router and the weak area than inside it.

In tri-band kits, one radio is kept for the backhaul alone, so your devices do not compete with the link between nodes. When both ends have 6 GHz, the planner uses whichever band gives the stronger link.

sections.q: When is running a cable worth it?
sections.html:
Whenever there is a way: through an empty conduit, the ceiling or along the baseboard. With wired backhaul, a node delivers the full speed no matter how many walls or floors are in the way, and it can sit in the middle of the weak area instead of halfway there.

Cat 5e or Cat 6 cable is plenty for home internet. Most mesh kits accept a cable between nodes with no setup: just connect the network port of one to the other. When a cable is out of the question, powerline adapters are an alternative, but their speed varies a lot with the home’s wiring.

sections.q: When does an extender do the job?
sections.html:
When the problem is a single room close to an area that already has good signal, and the budget is tight. Place the extender where the router’s signal still arrives strong, not inside the dead room: it can only repeat what it receives.

Prefer dual-band models that receive on one band and transmit on the other, or ones with a network port so they can become a wired access point later. Avoid chaining extenders: every wireless hop loses speed again.

sections.q: Can I use an old router as an access point?
sections.html:
Yes, if it is connected to the main router with a cable. Set it to access point (AP) mode, with the same network name and password, and turn off its DHCP server. It works well to bring signal to a back room, a garage apartment or an upper floor.

The difference from mesh is roaming: with no coordination between the devices, your phone decides on its own when to switch, and sometimes it takes a while. If you stay put in one room, you will hardly notice.

sections.q: How do I compare the options in my home?
sections.html: Draw the floor plan, place the router where the modem is and a node in the weak area. The panel shows the link between the nodes in dBm. Then mark the node as Connected by network cable and see how much the map improves when it can go farther. If the wireless link is weak at every useful spot, the planner tells you that node needs a cable.

faq.q: Does mesh make my internet faster?
faq.a: It does not raise the speed of your plan. It brings good signal to more rooms; where the signal was already good, nothing changes.

faq.q: Can I connect mesh nodes with a cable?
faq.a: Yes, and it is the best of both worlds: the system keeps one network name and automatic roaming, and every wired node delivers the full speed.

faq.q: Can I use an extender together with mesh?
faq.a: Better not. The extender adds a hop the mesh does not control, and devices connected to it lose automatic roaming. One more mesh node covers the same room without those problems.

cta.title: Check the link between nodes
cta.text: Place the router and a node on your floor plan and check the link in dBm. Mark the node as wired to compare both options.

walls.title: How Much Do Walls and Floors Block Wi-Fi? Table in dB | Planejador WiFi
walls.description: Table of Wi-Fi signal loss per material at 2.4, 5 and 6 GHz: brick, concrete, drywall, glass, metal and floor slabs. Learn what a decibel is and how much each wall cuts range.
walls.h1: How much do walls and floors block Wi-Fi?
walls.answer:
On 5 GHz, a brick wall takes about {db.tijolo.b5} dB off the signal, a concrete wall {db.concreto.b5} dB, drywall {db.gesso.b5} dB and the concrete slab between floors {db.slab.b5} dB. Metal, mirrors and the fridge are the worst: {db.metal.b5} dB.

Every 10 dB lost leaves one tenth of the power. That is why a single concrete wall divides the distance at which signal stays good by {factor.b5.concreto}, and two brick walls take the range from {range.b5} m down to {range.b5.tijolo.2} m.

Higher bands lose more: the same brick wall takes {db.tijolo.b24} dB at 2.4 GHz and {db.tijolo.b6} dB at 6 GHz.

sections.q: How much does each material lose on each band?
sections.html:
Average values the planner uses, per wall crossed:

{table.materials}

Real loss changes with thickness, moisture and the steel inside the wall. A thick brick wall, or one with plaster that is still damp, can lose much more than the average; a thin partition, less.

sections.q: What is a decibel, in practice?
sections.html:
The decibel (dB) compares two power levels on a multiplying scale, not an adding one. The numbers that matter:

  • 3 dB: half the power.
  • 10 dB: one tenth.
  • 20 dB: one hundredth.

Losses in dB add up: two brick walls on 5 GHz take {db.tijolo.b5} + {db.tijolo.b5} dB, and every 10 dB of that sum divides the power by ten. In the model, going through one brick wall on 5 GHz costs as much as multiplying the distance by {factor.b5.tijolo}.

sections.q: Why do 5 and 6 GHz lose more through walls?
sections.html: The higher the frequency, the more the wave is absorbed by the wall materials. In the model, good signal through one brick wall reaches about {range.b24.tijolo} m on 2.4 GHz, {range.b5.tijolo} m on 5 GHz and {range.b6.tijolo} m on 6 GHz. On the other hand, the higher bands are much faster and less crowded, which is why they are worth it near the router.

sections.q: How much does the floor between stories block?
sections.html:
A concrete floor slab takes {db.slab.b24} dB at 2.4 GHz, {db.slab.b5} dB at 5 GHz and {db.slab.b6} dB at 6 GHz, almost as much as a concrete wall. The planner adds one slab per floor crossed and counts the {floorh} m between floors in the distance.

With the router downstairs, good 5 GHz signal reaches about {range.b5.slab} m upstairs in a straight line, before counting the walls up there. In homes with concrete floors, one node per floor is almost always worth it.

sections.q: Do doors, windows and mirrors make a difference?
sections.html:
• Wooden door: {db.madeira.b5} dB on 5 GHz when closed; nothing when open.
  • Plain glass: {db.vidro.b5} dB. Low-E or reflective glass has a metal coating and blocks much more.
  • Mirror: its backing is metal, and the model treats it as metal: {db.metal.b5} dB.
  • Aluminum sliding door, garage door and metal shower enclosure: metal too.

sections.q: How do I tell what my wall is made of?
sections.html: Knock on it: a hollow sound means drywall or a light partition. Columns and beams are concrete, and in many buildings the inner walls are load-bearing masonry that cannot be taken down; in the planner, treat both as concrete. Tiled kitchen and bathroom walls follow the wall behind the tiles. When torn between two materials, pick the heavier one: the result stays on the safe side.

faq.q: Does a thicker wall block more?
faq.a: Yes. The values in the table are for walls of usual thickness in homes. The planner uses one value per material, not per thickness, so a very thick wall can be drawn as concrete to get closer to reality.

faq.q: Do tiles or paint block Wi-Fi?
faq.a: Ordinary paint changes almost nothing, and tiles add little. What matters is the wall behind them and any metal: plaster mesh, foil-backed insulation, pipes or a steel cabinet against the wall.

faq.q: Can Wi-Fi go through a concrete wall?
faq.a: It can, but it loses a lot: {db.concreto.b5} dB on 5 GHz. In the model, good signal reaches about {range.b5.concreto} m past one concrete wall on 5 GHz and {range.b24.concreto} m on 2.4 GHz.

cta.title: Draw each wall with the right material
cta.text: In the planner, every wall has a material. Switch brick to concrete or glass and see right away how much the signal map changes.

dbm.title: Wi-Fi Signal Strength in dBm: What Is Good? | Planejador WiFi
dbm.description: What Wi-Fi signal strength in dBm means, why the number is negative, which value is good for video and gaming, and how to measure it on a phone or computer.
dbm.h1: What does Wi-Fi signal strength in dBm mean?
dbm.answer:
dBm is the power of the signal that reaches your device, compared with 1 milliwatt. For Wi-Fi the value is always negative, and the closer to zero, the better: {level.0} dBm or better is excellent, {level.0} to {level.1} dBm is good, and below {level.3} dBm the connection drops often.

Aim for {level.1} dBm or better in the rooms you use. That is the level where HD video and video calls run without freezing.

Small differences in the number are big in power: {level.1} dBm carries {ratio.1.3} times more power than {level.3} dBm.

sections.q: What is a good Wi-Fi signal in dBm?
sections.html:
{table.signal}

These are the ranges the planner uses to color the map. They apply to the signal a device receives; for the link between two mesh nodes the target is different: {link.1} dBm or better.

sections.q: Why is the number negative?
sections.html:
Because 0 dBm is 1 milliwatt, and the signal that reaches your phone is a tiny fraction of that. A mesh node transmits at around {tx.b5} dBm, about {mw.b5} mW. After a few meters and walls, something like −60 dBm reaches your device: one millionth of a milliwatt.

The scale moves in steps of 10: −30 dBm is one thousandth of a milliwatt, −40 dBm is ten times less than that, and so on. Every 3 dB lower is half the power.

sections.q: dBm, bars or percentage: which one counts?
sections.html: dBm does. Your phone’s bars and the percentage in Windows are conversions each maker does its own way: three bars on one device can be two on another, with the same signal. dBm is the real measure, and it is what Wi-Fi analyzer apps show as RSSI.

sections.q: How do I measure signal strength in dBm?
sections.html:
• Android: install a Wi-Fi analyzer app; it shows the dBm of your network and the neighbors’.
  • iPhone: iOS does not show dBm in Settings. Install Apple’s AirPort Utility, turn on “Wi-Fi Scanner” under Settings › AirPort Utility and run a scan.
  • Mac: hold the Option key and click the Wi-Fi icon; the value shows as RSSI.
  • Windows: the system shows a percentage, not dBm. A Wi-Fi analyzer app shows the value in dBm.

Measure standing still, with the device in your hand, where you usually use it, and repeat a few times: the value moves a few dB from one second to the next.

sections.q: Does a strong signal guarantee fast internet?
sections.html: No. dBm tells you how much signal arrives, not how much noise comes with it. In a building with dozens of networks on the same channel, a {level.1} dBm signal can deliver less than a {level.2} dBm signal in a detached house. Speed also depends on your plan, your device and the channel width. Good signal is a requirement for fast internet, but not enough on its own.

sections.q: Why does my phone show signal but the connection fails?
sections.html: Because Wi-Fi is a two-way street. Your phone transmits with much less power than the router, so at the edge of coverage it still hears the router, but the router no longer hears it well. The signal looks fine and pages do not load. That is why it pays to aim for {level.1} dBm or better, not for the last spot where the phone still shows the network.

faq.q: Is −50 dBm better than −70 dBm?
faq.a: Yes. The closer to zero, the stronger: −50 dBm carries a hundred times more power than −70 dBm.

faq.q: What signal do I need for online gaming?
faq.a: Aim for {level.0} dBm or better. Games depend more on stability and latency than on speed, and a strong signal reduces the retransmissions that cause lag spikes. For a console or desktop computer, a network cable is better still.

faq.q: What is RSSI?
faq.a: It stands for received signal strength indicator. In analyzer apps and on the Mac, RSSI is shown in dBm and is the same number as on this page.

cta.text: Draw your home and the planner colors every spot with the same dBm ranges as this page, on 2.4, 5 and 6 GHz.

bands.title: 2.4 vs 5 vs 6 GHz: Which Wi-Fi Band Should You Use? | Planejador WiFi
bands.description: The difference between 2.4 GHz, 5 GHz and 6 GHz Wi-Fi in range, speed and walls, when a 6 GHz router (Wi-Fi 6E and Wi-Fi 7) is worth it and which device to put on each band.
bands.h1: 2.4, 5 or 6 GHz: which Wi-Fi band should you use?
bands.answer:
Use 5 GHz day to day: it is much faster than 2.4 GHz and reaches most of the house with one or two nodes. 2.4 GHz goes farther and gets through walls better, but it is slow and crowded. 6 GHz is the fastest and least crowded, with the shortest range.

In the model, with no walls in the way, good signal reaches about {range.b24} m on 2.4 GHz, {range.b5} m on 5 GHz and {range.b6} m on 6 GHz. Through one brick wall: {range.b24.tijolo}, {range.b5.tijolo} and {range.b6.tijolo} m.

You do not have to pick one. With the same network name on every band, the router or mesh moves each device to the best one at the time.

sections.q: Which band reaches farthest?
sections.html:
2.4 GHz, by a wide margin. Distance at which signal stays good ({level.1} dBm or better), in the model:

  • Two brick walls: {range.b24.tijolo.2} m on 2.4 GHz, {range.b5.tijolo.2} m on 5 GHz and {range.b6.tijolo.2} m on 6 GHz.
  • One concrete wall: {range.b24.concreto} m, {range.b5.concreto} m and {range.b6.concreto} m.
  • Floor slab, straight up to the next floor: {range.b24.slab} m, {range.b5.slab} m and {range.b6.slab} m.

That is why, in a far room, your phone sometimes prefers 2.4 GHz: it is slower, but it gets there.

sections.q: Which band is fastest?
sections.html:
Speed depends on the channel width and on how many networks compete for the same space.

  • 2.4 GHz: only three non-overlapping channels and, in practice, narrow 20 MHz channels. It shares the air with neighbors, Bluetooth and microwave ovens.
  • 5 GHz: many more channels and widths up to 160 MHz. It is the main band on most routers.
  • 6 GHz: the newest band, still lightly used, with 160 MHz channels and, on Wi-Fi 7, 320 MHz.

With good signal, 5 and 6 GHz deliver several times the speed of 2.4 GHz. With weak signal, that edge disappears.

sections.q: Is a 6 GHz router worth it?
sections.html:
It is if you have compatible devices (Wi-Fi 6E or Wi-Fi 7) and use them near the nodes, or if the mesh kit will use 6 GHz to link one node to the next. In that role the band shines: it is free of device traffic and has plenty of width. When both ends of a link have 6 GHz, the planner compares both bands and uses whichever gives the stronger link.

If there are many walls between the nodes, the 6 GHz link can get too weak and the kit falls back to 5 GHz. For internet up to 1 Gbps and older devices, a dual-band mesh is usually enough. In the United States, the FCC opened the 6 GHz band to Wi-Fi in 2020.

sections.q: Which device goes on which band?
sections.html:
• 2.4 GHz: smart bulbs, plugs, cameras and other smart-home devices; many only work on this band. It also suits devices at the far end of the yard.
  • 5 GHz: phones, laptops, TVs and game consoles. It is the default band for almost everything.
  • 6 GHz: new devices that sit near the router or a node, like a work laptop or a VR headset.

sections.q: Should I split the 2.4 and 5 GHz networks?
sections.html: Usually not. With a single name, the router handles the band switching itself (band steering) and your phone does not get stuck on 2.4 GHz when it is close by. Split them only if a smart-home device fails to set up on the combined network; in that case, create an extra 2.4 GHz network just for it.

sections.q: How do I see each band on my floor plan?
sections.html: In the planner, switch between 2.4, 5 and 6 GHz at the top of the map. The same plan, with the same nodes, shows the reach of each band and the share of the house with good signal. Start with 5 GHz: if it covers the rooms you use, the house is well served.

faq.q: Why doesn’t my phone show the 6 GHz network?
faq.a: The 6 GHz band only shows up on devices with Wi-Fi 6E or Wi-Fi 7, with an up-to-date system, in a country that has opened the band. Phones with plain Wi-Fi 6 see only 2.4 and 5 GHz.

faq.q: Does 5 GHz go through floors?
faq.a: It does, but it loses {db.slab.b5} dB, against {db.slab.b24} dB on 2.4 GHz. In the model, good 5 GHz signal reaches about {range.b5.slab} m on the floor above, before the walls up there.

faq.q: Wi-Fi 6, 6E and 7: what is the difference in bands?
faq.a: Wi-Fi 6 uses 2.4 and 5 GHz. Wi-Fi 6E adds 6 GHz. Wi-Fi 7 uses all three, with wider channels at 6 GHz and the option to use more than one band at the same time.

methodology.title: Methodology: How Planejador WiFi Estimates Signal | Planejador WiFi
methodology.description: The planner’s propagation model: distance loss with exponent {n}, wall and floor loss on each band, backhaul quality, how Suggest a spot works and the limits of the estimate.
methodology.lead:
Planejador WiFi estimates the signal at every point of the floor plan with a simple propagation model: loss grows with the logarithm of distance, and every wall or floor slab crossed adds a fixed loss that depends on the material and the band. The math runs in your browser, and the code is open source.

The result has a typical error of ±8 dB. Use it to compare placements and decide how many nodes to buy, not to replace an on-site measurement.

sections.html:
The signal at a point is the device’s power minus the loss along the way:

signal = power + model adjustment − [PL0 + 10 · n · log10(d) + walls + floors × slab]

  • d is the distance in meters between the node and the point, in three dimensions: between floors it counts {floorh} m per floor. Distances under half a meter count as half a meter.
  • n = {n} is the distance loss exponent.
  • PL0 is the loss at 1 m, equal to the free-space loss at the band’s reference frequency: 20 · log10(f in MHz) − 27.55.
  • Model adjustment is each router’s power relative to a typical mesh node; models you add have this adjustment too.
{table.bands}

The site-general indoor model in Recommendation ITU-R P.1238 has the same form but no wall term: the effect of walls is folded into its distance coefficient. Here every wall is counted one by one, so the exponent stays closer to the free-space value of 2.

sections.h: Loss per wall, material and band
sections.html:
For each point, the planner draws a straight line to every node and adds the loss of each wall the line crosses. A corner shared by two walls counts once. For a point on another floor, it adds one slab per floor crossed and the walls of the floor the point is on.

{table.materials}

These are average values for homes. Laboratory measurements, such as NIST’s in report NISTIR 6055, show that the loss of the same material varies widely with thickness and frequency. The planner uses one value per material and ignores the drawn thickness.

The map colors every point in five levels, from excellent ({level.0} dBm or better) to no usable signal (below {level.3} dBm). The full table is in the dBm guide. Each point takes the signal of the strongest node.

The coverage percentage is the share of the area at {level.1} dBm or better, computed on a {grid} m grid inside the rectangle around the floor’s walls.

The wireless link between two nodes uses the same calculation, with the adjustment of the weaker of the two devices and the walls of both floors when they are on different floors. If both have 6 GHz, the planner works out the link on 5 and on 6 GHz and keeps the stronger one; otherwise it uses 5 GHz.

  • {link.0} dBm or better: great.
  • {link.0} to {link.1} dBm: good.
  • Below {link.1} dBm: weak; the planner recommends a cable.

Wired nodes hang from the main router. The others join the network one at a time, through the strongest link to a node already in it, which builds a tree with no loops and the router at its root.

1. It splits the floor’s rectangle into a {suggest.cell} m grid and drops points closer than {suggest.wallGap} m to a wall.
  2. For each point, it imagines a new node there and works out the area at {level.1} dBm or better, together with the existing nodes.
  3. If there are nodes already, it only accepts points with a wireless link of {link.1} dBm or better to one of them. When no useful point meets that, it tries again without the requirement and warns that the node will need a cable.
  4. It keeps the point that adds the most covered area. Ties go to the higher sum of signal over all points, counting at least {suggest.floor} dBm at each.

If no point improves coverage by at least one percentage point, the planner says why: the house is already covered, no point helps, or a link between nodes is weak and needs a cable.

The typical error is ±8 dB. The model leaves out:

  • reflections and signal that goes around walls through doors and hallways;
  • furniture, people, appliances and water, unless you draw them as walls;
  • interference from neighboring networks, Bluetooth and microwave ovens;
  • the antenna and power of each phone or laptop, which transmit less than the router;
  • open or closed doors, the real thickness of walls and the steel inside them;
  • speed: the planner estimates signal, not megabits.

Use the map to compare placements and kits on the same floor plan. After installing, measure the signal in the rooms that matter and adjust.

The guides quote rectangular homes drawn by the site itself: brick outer walls, rooms of about {room} × {room} m and a {door} m wooden door in every inner wall. Nodes are placed one by one with the same search as Suggest a spot, on 5 GHz, until each floor has good signal over at least {target} of its area. The numbers are recalculated every time the site is published.

• ITU-R. Recommendation P.1238: Propagation data and prediction methods for the planning of indoor radiocommunication systems.
  • Stone, W. C. Electromagnetic Signal Attenuation in Construction Materials, NISTIR 6055. NIST, 1997.
  • Model code: assets/js/engine.js, in the Planejador WiFi repository on GitHub.

about.title: About the project | Planejador WiFi
about.description: What Planejador WiFi is, who it is for, how it works under the hood, and how to report a bug or suggest an improvement.
about.lead: Planejador WiFi is a Wi-Fi coverage calculator for houses and apartments. The idea is simple: try it on the floor plan before you buy, to see where the router should go and how many mesh nodes your home needs.

sections.html:
For anyone about to buy a router or a mesh kit who wants to get it right the first time. You don't need to know what dBm or backhaul mean: the map shows coverage in colors, and the technical details are there for anyone who wants them.

Networking enthusiasts can adjust materials, bands and router models. Installers can put together a quick estimate for a client and send the exported project.

For large offices, warehouses or networks with many access points, the right approach is an on-site survey with proper equipment.

sections.h: How it works under the hood
sections.html:
All the math runs in your browser. There is no sign-up, and your project never goes to a server: it stays in your browser, as the privacy policy explains.

The estimate comes from a propagation model that adds up the loss over distance and through each wall in the way; the methodology shows the formula and the values. The numbers quoted in the guides come from the same code that draws the map, so the guides and the planner don't disagree.
Planejador WiFi doesn't sell any equipment. The built-in router models, from several brands, are a starting point for comparison, and you can add your own model if it isn't on the list.
The code is on GitHub under the MIT license: anyone can read, copy and adapt it. The site is available in Portuguese, English and Spanish, and each language has its own URLs.

Seeing an odd result, a bug or a bad translation? Open an issue on GitHub or email contato@planejadorwifi.com. Measurements from real homes help calibrate the model, and code contributions are welcome: the contributing guide explains how.

Please don't report security issues in a public issue: use GitHub's private vulnerability reporting, on the repository's Security tab.
